**In Praise of Paying Attention**

If you asked me to describe what I have actually done with my life, I would be in some trouble. I could give you the copy of my resume, which is tidy and chronological and full of verbs that sound impressively active. I have coordinated, I have managed, I have contributed. I have lived in three cities, owned two cars, learned to file taxes in two different countries. But none of that feels true in the way that matters. What I remember, stubbornly and against all good sense, are things that would never make it onto a resume. The exact blue of the sky at 6:14 on a Tuesday in October when I was waiting for a bus that never came. The sound my grandmother made when she laughed and then coughed a little at the end of it. The smell of rain hitting hot pavement outside a library in a town I cannot name anymore. My life, as I have actually lived it, has been made out of small, unrecorded moments of attention, and everything else has been filler between them.

I have come to believe that attention is the rarest and most generous thing a person can offer. Not love, not money, not even time exactly, because time can be wasted on someone you are not really seeing. Attention is different. Attention is where you put your mind, willingly, and keep it there. It is a form of hospitality. When you truly look at something — a face, a tree, a cup of tea, a problem that has been bothering you for weeks — you are making room for it inside yourself. You are saying, for this minute, you are more important than my distraction. In a world that is engineered, with astonishing ingenuity, to steal that minute away from you, to pay attention has become a slightly radical act. It is slow. It is inconvenient. It does not scale. And it is, I suspect, the only thing that ever really changes us.

I notice it first in the mornings. I am not a morning person by nature; I am someone who has to be dragged, gently and with coffee, into the day. But there is a specific hour, just before the house fully wakes up, when the light does something that I have never been able to photograph properly. It comes in low and sideways through the kitchen window, and it falls across the table in a way that makes even a chipped mug look like it belongs in a museum. The dust is visible in it, turning slowly. For about ten minutes, nothing has asked anything of me yet. No phone has buzzed. No news cycle has arrived to tell me what I should be angry about. It's just light and quiet and the faint hum of the refrigerator. I used to scroll through those ten minutes. Now I try to sit in them. I watch the light move a fraction of an inch across the wood. I listen to the birds decide whether to be loud today. It is a very small practice, almost nothing, but it has taught me that the day does not have to start with urgency. It can start with noticing.

From noticing, other things follow. When you actually look at your kitchen, you start to see how many objects in it have a history. The wooden spoon with the burned tip belonged to my mother, who burned everything she cooked in the first three years of marriage and then became a very good cook out of sheer embarrassment. The blue bowl is from a thrift store in Portland, and I bought it because it reminded me of the bowl I had as a child, which was also blue but had a chip shaped exactly like the state of Texas. I did not know it was shaped like Texas until I was twenty and eating cereal very slowly during a depressive episode. These are not useful facts. They are not going to improve my productivity or my net worth. They are just the way a life accretes, like barnacles on a hull, until one day you realize you are carrying a whole ecosystem with you and calling it home.

Memory is a strange editor. I have forgotten most of what I learned in high school chemistry, and I have forgotten the names of most people I was once certain I would never forget. But I remember, with damp clarity, the summer I was eleven and my family rented a house near the coast for three weeks because my father had been laid off and we decided, in a fit of optimism that now seems deranged, to treat unemployment as a vacation. We had almost no money. We ate a lot of pasta. We swam every day at a beach that was too cold for swimming. I learned to read the tide charts in the newspaper, not because anyone taught me, but because the newspaper was the only thing in the house that arrived every day and I was bored. I remember the way the fog would come in at four in the afternoon and erase the world beyond the front porch. I remember my parents whispering on that porch after we were supposed to be asleep, trying to be hopeful in that low, adult voice that children pretend not to hear. I think that summer taught me something I still use: you can be broke and frightened and still have a good time, provided you are paying attention to the fog.

Paying attention, I have learned, is not the same as being vigilant. Vigilance is scanning for threats. Attention is opening your hands. One is tense, the other is soft. When I walk now, which I do more than I used to, I am trying to practice the soft version. I live in a neighborhood that many people describe as "nice," which is a word that means there is nothing particularly interesting about it. The houses are similar. The trees are mature but unremarkable. There is a Starbucks on the corner and a dog park that smells faintly of old decisions. And yet, if I walk the same loop at different hours, it becomes a different place entirely. At seven in the morning, there is an elderly man who walks his corgi and talks to it in a very serious tone, as if negotiating a treaty. At noon, there is a group of teenagers who have claimed the bus stop as their parliament, and they argue about music with the passion of Supreme Court justices. At dusk, the windows light up one by one, and you can see the silhouettes of people making dinner, washing dishes, living the one wild and precious life in small domestic frames. Nothing happens, and everything happens. It depends entirely on whether you are looking.

I think we are afraid of looking too closely because we suspect that if we do, we will have to admit how much we miss. We will notice the crack in the sidewalk where someone once fell. We will notice that our friend has been quieter lately. We will notice that we are, in fact, getting older, and that the smell of that particular sunscreen will forever be associated with a person who is no longer in our lives. Attention brings grief with it, because to see clearly is to see that everything changes. But I think that is the bargain worth making. The alternative — drifting through your one life like a tourist in your own hometown, photographing nothing, remembering nothing — seems far more frightening. I would rather be sad about a real moment than numb about a lost one.

Work, for all its importance, is where attention goes to die if you let it. I have had jobs that required me to be incredibly focused and jobs that required me to be incredibly distracted, and the second kind was more damaging. When you spend eight hours a day splitting your mind between fourteen tabs and a Slack channel and a vague sense of dread, you come home feeling exhausted in a way that sleep does not fix. It is a particular kind of tiredness that comes from never fully arriving anywhere. Lately, I have been trying to build small rituals of single-mindedness into my workday. I make tea and I drink it without looking at a screen. I write one paragraph of a difficult email and then I stand up and look out the window for thirty seconds. I keep a paper notebook on my desk, not for efficiency, but because writing by hand forces me to commit to a thought long enough to finish it. These are tiny resistances, but they add up. The brain, like a muscle, remembers how it is used. Use it for skimming, and it will skim everything. Use it for noticing, and it will start to notice on its own, even when you are not trying.

Cooking has been my great teacher in this regard. I was not raised by cooks. My mother could make exactly five meals, and we rotated through them with grim loyalty. I learned to cook in my thirties, mostly out of necessity and a desire to impress people I ended up not liking very much. But what I discovered, very slowly, is that cooking is attention made edible. You cannot pay half attention to a pan of onions. If you walk away, they burn. If you stare at them too hard, they feel judged and also burn. You have to be present in a kind of relaxed way, stirring, tasting, adjusting, listening to the sound it makes. The sound changes. Good cooks listen to food. I am not a good cook, but I am an attentive one, and that has been enough to feed myself and occasionally my friends in a way that feels like care. There is a pot of soup that I make every winter, just beans and carrots and garlic and whatever greens are on sale, and when I make it, the whole apartment smells like perseverance. I think that is a good smell. I think perseverance should smell like that.

Rain is another teacher. I grew up in a place where it rained for seven months a year, and for a long time I resented it. Rain meant wet socks and mildew and the particular gloom that settles on a town when the sun has been absent so long that people start to name the clouds. Now I live somewhere with a proper summer, and I find I miss the rain in a way that surprises me. When it does rain, I try to be awake for it. I open the windows a crack so I can hear it properly. I walk in it without an umbrella if I can, just to feel it on my face and remember that weather is not personal. It is not rewarding you or punishing you. It is just there, doing what it does, and your job is to decide whether you will be inside being annoyed about it or outside being wet and briefly, improbably alive. I have made a lot of bad decisions in my life, but I have never regretted going for a walk in the rain.

Reading is attention at a longer distance. I read a lot of novels, but the books that have stayed with me are the ones that taught me how to notice other minds. I remember reading a passage in a book by a writer I love where a character, an old woman, is watching her granddaughter sleep and thinking about how love is mostly just witnessing. I had to put the book down and go look at my own life for a minute. I think good writing does that: it slows you down enough to see the person in the next room more clearly. I also have a box of old letters, from my grandmother mostly, that I keep in a closet. I do not read them often. I could not bear to. But every few years I take one out, and I am moved not so much by what she says — she was a practical woman who mostly wrote about weather and vegetables — but by the fact that she took the time to say it. She paid attention to the weather. She paid attention to the vegetables. She wrote it down. That, I think, is a complete philosophy of life, if you are willing to accept it.

Music is trickier. I love music, but I am bad at listening to it properly. I tend to use it as background, as a way to fill silence while I do other things. Recently, I have been trying to listen to one album at a time, sitting down, doing nothing else. It is harder than it sounds. The mind wants to wander. The phone wants to be checked. But if I stay, something wonderful happens around the third song. The music stops being a soundtrack and becomes a place I am in. I notice the bass line, which I have never noticed before. I notice the moment where the singer takes a breath before the chorus and decides, very slightly, to do it differently. I notice that I have been holding my shoulders up around my ears for the entire day and that I can put them down now. Music, listened to with attention, is like a friend who has come over and is telling you a long story that is not really about events, but about feeling. You do not need to do anything but receive it.

Talking to strangers is a lost art, and I mourn it. There was a time when you would chat with the person next to you on a train, or in line for coffee, and you would learn something small and true about a life entirely unlike your own. Now we have headphones and screens and a general agreement that strangers are threats until proven otherwise. I understand the reasons for this, especially for women, especially at night, but I still miss the casual generosity of it. I had a conversation last year with a man at a laundromat who told me he folded other people's laundry by accident once and decided he liked the feeling of being needed, so he started a folding service. He was not joking. He was a very serious man about folding. I think about him every time I fold a fitted sheet, which is to say, I think about him often and with great fondness. He paid attention to something small — the satisfaction of a well-folded shirt — and built a small life around it. I would like to be more like him.

Time is the great thief, everyone says, but I think time is more like a great editor. It cuts. It removes scenes that you thought were essential. It keeps one line of dialogue from a conversation you had twenty years ago and deletes the entire afternoon around it. I have tried to make peace with this by keeping a different kind of record. Not photographs, exactly — I have thousands of photographs, and they increasingly feel like evidence that I was somewhere I did not fully inhabit. I mean a record of attention. I keep a small notebook where I write down, once a week, one thing I noticed. Not a gratitude list, not a to-do list. Just a noticing. The way the light hit the grocery store parking lot on Thursday. The way my neighbor laughs. The way coffee tastes different when it is the first cup and you have not yet read the news. These entries are worthless to anyone else. They are also, I suspect, the most valuable thing I own, because they prove to me that I was here, and that I was awake.

Aging, which I am now doing in earnest, is a lesson in attention whether you want it or not. Your body starts to send you very specific messages. Your knees comment on the weather. Your back has opinions about chairs. Your eyes do not focus as quickly as they used to, which has the paradoxical effect of making you look more carefully at things, holding them a little farther away, squinting a little. I find myself listening harder in conversations, not because my hearing is bad, but because I understand, in a way I did not at twenty-five, that I will not have unlimited chances to hear this person say this thing. My parents are older now. When I talk to my mother on the phone, I pay attention to the pauses. She has always paused before answering a question, as if consulting an internal committee. I used to fill those pauses with my own chatter. Now I let them be. In them, I can hear her deciding how honest to be. It is a small sound, but it is the sound of a whole person thinking.

And so I come back to the beginning, to the idea that a life is made of attention. I do not want to be a person who traveled the world and saw nothing. I do not want to be a person who had a thousand friends and knew none of them. I want to be a person who, when asked what she did with her one wild and precious life, can point to a kitchen table in the morning light and say, I sat there. I watched. I listened. I made soup. I wrote it down. I missed people terribly and I loved them anyway, and I tried, most days, to be actually present for the brief, astonishing fact of being alive in a particular place, at a particular time, with particular people who would not be here forever.

It is not a grand ambition. It will not be on my resume. But I think it might be enough.
